articles.title: India-US joint narco bust: Investigators find arrested man deported from US in drug case
articles.summary: New Delhi: Investigation into a recent cross-border drug trafficking racket unearthed by the NCB and the US DEA has found that one of the arrested Indians was deported a few years ago from the United States in a drug case, while some of the other accused were highly educated, holding MBA and B.Tech degrees. Officials told PTI that the joint probe into the case, in which six Indians were arrested following multi-city raids between November 4-13, has been enlarged and the accused are being questioned about their linkages and alleged illegal dealings. They said the accused, T Manoj, a Telangana resident, was deported from the US in January 2024 for allegedly trading certain regulated drugs. The 27-year-old has a B.Tech in Computer Science and was pursuing a Master's degree in the US. 208 kg of drugs seized in Tamil Nadu in a month were bound for Sri Lanka, investigators say Investigators are examining his linkages in the US and India. Another accused is 30-year-old T D Jaiswal, a Lucknow resident who holds an MBA degree and has business links with a pharmacy and a clothing store in the Uttar Pradesh capital, according to investigators. Arti Soni, 32, from Lucknow, is a Mathematics graduate who worked in corporate event management, while A Muttalib, 28, from Kolkata, holds an engineering degree and was engaged in cloth manufacturing and the dairy business. D K Tiwari, 39, an arts graduate, allegedly has business links with Jaiswal, while Jaswant, 29, studied up to Class 12 and worked as an electrician in Lucknow, according to officials. Multiple opioid medicines like Xanax (Alprazolam), Ativan, Tramadol, Valium (Diazepam) and Ambien are suspected to have been shipped from India to customers in the US as part of this alleged transnational drug ring, which the NCB and the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) busted jointly in an operation codenamed "Monsoon Thunder". The NCB said in a statement on November 20 that records and digital evidence examined so far indicate that the network handled close to 3,000 parcels containing nearly five lakh tablets across the US between June 2022 and November 2026. Customer databases of more than 59,000 subjects, which include transactions, details of past consignments, delivery addresses, USPS (United States Postal Service) tracking IDs, and drug types, have also been shared with the DEA to help them identify the customers and drop-shippers operating in the US, according to NCB. The NCB found that Indian operators received drug orders through online platforms like Telegram, Skype and WhatsApp. Consignments were dispatched through postal and other delivery channels, including the USPS, by the network operating in the US. Payments were received through digital platforms such as Venmo, a US-based payment app, bank accounts held in other persons' names, UPI and cryptocurrency, the agency said. Union Home Minister Amit Shah called the joint operation an "exemplary success," while US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor described it as "a great example of the US-India partnership in action".

The school was closed for the Deepavali holidays at the time of the incident and was noticed after the school reopened. The school headmaster lodged a complaint with the Udayarpalayam police and the school education department officials over the incident. Subsequently, another group led by VCK Ariyalur east district secretary Kadirvalavan entered the collectorate and staged a protest at the portico, raising slogans against the police and school education department officials. The protests led to tense moments at the collectorate, which was witnessing the weekly grievance redressal meeting. articles.title: Christian nuns and priests are entitled to share in ancestral property, says Kerala HC
articles.summary: A woman does not lose her right to inherit ancestral property merely by becoming a nun, the Kerala High Court has ruled, rejecting a man's plea to deny his sister a share in compensation awarded for the acquisition of their father's land. The court held that entering a religious order does not amount to 'civil death' or extinguish a person's inheritance rights under Indian law. Justice G Girish dismissed a petition filed by 66-year-old Jose AM of Kozhikode, who challenged an order directing the equal distribution of Rs 3.74 crore in land acquisition compensation among him and his five siblings. The Land Acquisition Rehabilitation and Resettlement Authority (Additional District Court-IV), Kozhikode, had ruled that, as per the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, all six siblings were entitled to the compensation amount of Rs 3.74 crore awarded following the government’s acquisition of 3.295 acres of land that used to belong to their father. Jose had argued that one of his sisters, who had become a nun, was no longer entitled to inherit the family property. The court relied on Supreme Court and Kerala High Court judgements to reiterate that religious renunciation does not automatically deprive Christian priests or nuns of their inheritance rights under the Indian Succession Act, 1925. It also rejected his other arguments, including that siblings who had moved away from their ancestral home were not entitled to solatium and that another brother had relinquished his share through an unregistered family settlement. All heirs have equal claim to solatium Jose had argued that his siblings were not entitled to a share of the solatium as they had not experienced the pain and suffering associated with the acquisition. He also contended that one of his brothers had relinquished his rights over the family property through a 2009 family settlement agreement, while one of his sisters, having become a nun, had effectively undergone 'civil death' and could no longer claim inheritance. Rejecting the arguments, the High Court observed that the attachment to ancestral property does not disappear simply because family members move away from their parental home. "It may be true that the respondents 4 to 8 (siblings) might be residing away from the acquired property pursuant to their shifting from their parental home during the course of their life. But, that does not mean that their emotional attachment with their ancestral property would have been lost by such shifting," the court said. The petitioner had argued that he deserved a greater share of the compensation because he lived near the acquired property and had been managing it until the acquisition. The court, however, said this did not give him any special entitlement over the compensation or solatium. It observed that his management of the property was an act performed on behalf of all the co-owners. "There is no basis for the contention that the aforesaid act of the petitioner taking care of the ancestral property for and on behalf of the co-owners of that property would confer him any special right to have exclusive allotment of solatium," Justice Girish said. Quoting Wharton's Law Lexicon, the judgement described solatium as "an expression of solace or a compassionate allowance given to a person to mitigate the hardship, inconvenience, or emotional pain caused by an involuntary act, such as the forced taking of their property." The judgement pointed out that the petitioner could not claim to have suffered greater emotional trauma than his siblings merely because he had been looking after the property. Unregistered family settlement cannot extinguish property rights On the petitioner's contention that his brother, the fourth respondent, had relinquished his rights through a family settlement agreement dated August 29, 2009, the court found that the document was legally invalid because it had not been registered. The court explained that a family arrangement requires registration if it creates or extinguishes rights in immovable property. A mere memorandum recording an arrangement already arrived at between family members may be exempt from registration, as it does not independently create or extinguish such rights. However, the court found that the agreement in question sought to extinguish the brother's rights over the family property itself. "It is apparent from the said document that the extinguishment of the right of the fourth respondent over the family property was sought to be created by the said document," the judgement said. Referring to Sections 17 and 49 of the Registration Act, the court held that the agreement was compulsorily registrable and could not be relied upon in legal proceedings without registration. Becoming a nun does not mean losing inheritance rights The High Court also rejected the argument that the sixth respondent, who is a nun, was disqualified from inheriting the compensation amount. The petitioner had contended that becoming a nun amounted to 'civil death', thereby depriving her of her rights over the family property. Rejecting this argument, the court relied on the Supreme Court's judgement in Molly Joseph v. George Sebastian (1997), which held that laws enacted by the legislature prevail over personal laws, usages, or customs. The court noted that the Indian Succession Act, 1925, does not create any exception to inheritance rights in the case of Christian priests or nuns. It also referred to a 2017 Division Bench judgement of the Kerala High Court in Monsignor Xavier Chullikkal and Others v. CG Raphel and Others , which held that entering a religious order and renouncing worldly pleasures does not automatically deprive a person of property acquired through intestate or testamentary succession. The same legal position was subsequently followed by the High Court in Mariyam @ Beatrice v. Father Joseph Mattam (Died) (2024). "The mere fact that one has entered into a religious order and renounced his worldly pleasures would not automatically result in the deprivation of property acquired by way of intestate or testamentary succession," the court reiterated. Finding all three grounds raised by the petitioner unsustainable, Justice Girish concluded that the writ petition was devoid of merit and dismissed it.

articles.title: FIR filed against TVK MLA Arul Vignesh, woman IAS officer also files POSH complaint
articles.summary: The Tamil Nadu police have registered a case against Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) MLA C Arul Vignesh over a complaint by a District Collector alleging sexual harassment. The case was registered on Tuesday, November 24, following the intervention of the Madras High Court which questioned the authorities’ handling of the complaint. TNM has also learnt that on November 23, the woman officer sent a written complaint to state Chief Secretary M Sai Kumar under the PoSH Act (Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013). The developments in the court came a day after the state told the court that neither the police nor the Chief Secretary had received a formal complaint from the Collector. However, on November 24 Tuesday, the state informed the court that the alleged conduct had been brought to the authorities’ attention a few months ago and that a complaint had since been received on November 23 and a case registered. TNM has learnt that the MLA has been booked under provisions of Section 75 (sexual harassment) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023 and section 132 (assault or using criminal force to deter a public servant from discharging their duty). The court has said that a Superintendent of Police-rank officer would conduct the probe, while an Inspector General of Police-rank officer would supervise it. The allegations first drew public attention earlier this month, when reports said Arul Vignesh had sent the Collector messages and made unwanted advances at public events. There were also allegations that he had attempted to enter her official residence. The MLA denied sending inappropriate messages and described the allegations as politically motivated. CTR Nirmal Kumar, the Minister for Law even went to the extent of denying the incident and questioned DMK leader Kanimozhi for issuing a statement about it. “Nothing happened as claimed by her. The issue was picked up by the media. Can I make allegations against her (Kanimozhi) just because something has appeared on social media? She is the starting point. How can she do that? She has the right to call the person concerned and clarify,” he told reporters on November 12. However, on November 15, the National Commission for Women (NCW) had taken suo motu cognisance of the allegations following a TNM report published on November 11. The Commission sought an impartial inquiry by the Tamil Nadu Director General of Police and a detailed Action Taken Report within seven days. During Tuesday’s hearing, the judge questioned why no action had been taken for months despite the authorities being informed of the alleged incident. The judge told the State Public Prosecutor not to protect anyone and directed that an Internal Complaints Committee (ICC) be formed to inquire into the Collector’s complaint. The judge said the committee should include members from outside the IAS cadre. “Let not just IAS officers be a part of it. There should be others too. The judge also says, had the intrusions abated, the victim woman IAS officer might not have lodged the complaint yesterday,” the judge said, according to The Hindu. The court also directed the police to act against people posting abusive content about the officer on social media. The judge observed that the officer might not have filed a complaint had the alleged intrusions stopped. The judge ordered that the officer’s name be withheld from the copy of the order uploaded to the High Court website and replaced with “XXXX” to protect her identity. The court decided to record Tuesday’s proceedings and adjourned the case to Friday, November 27, when it will seek an update on the police investigation and the composition of the ICC.

His death is tragic, and those who assaulted him must be held accountable, but the alleged stalking shouldn't be sanitised in the process. Stalking can turn dangerous, as the Anantapur chainsaw attack on a 15-year-old girl showed. Both facts matter, and neither should be erased.
